title: Alkanes
content:
# Alkanes

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Describe the structure and bonding in alkanes
- Name and draw alkanes with up to 5 carbon atoms
- Describe the physical properties of alkanes and their trends
- Write equations for the complete combustion of alkanes

## Introduction

**Alkanes** are the simplest hydrocarbons. They contain only carbon and hydrogen atoms, joined by single covalent bonds. They are the main components of natural gas and crude oil.

## Key Concepts

### What Are Alkanes?

**Alkanes are:**
- Hydrocarbons (contain only C and H)
- Saturated (only single bonds)
- General formula: **CₙH₂ₙ₊₂**

### The First Five Alkanes

| Name | Molecular formula | Structural formula | State at RTP |
|------|-------------------|--------------------|--------------|
| Methane | CH₄ | CH₄ | Gas |
| Ethane | C₂H₆ | CH₃CH₃ | Gas |
| Propane | C₃H₈ | CH₃CH₂CH₃ | Gas |
| Butane | C₄H₁₀ | CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ | Gas |
| Pentane | C₅H₁₂ | CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ | Liquid |

[DIAGRAM: Displayed formulae showing all C-H and C-C bonds for methane, ethane, propane, butane]

### Bonding in Alkanes

**Each carbon atom:**
- Forms 4 single covalent bonds
- Is bonded to other carbons and/or hydrogens
- Uses all 4 outer electrons in bonding

**Each hydrogen atom:**
- Forms 1 single covalent bond
- Shares 1 electron with carbon

**Structure:**
- Tetrahedral arrangement around each carbon
- Bond angle approximately 109.5°

### Physical Properties of Alkanes

| Property | Trend down the series |
|----------|----------------------|
| Boiling point | Increases |
| Melting point | Increases |
| Viscosity | Increases |
| Flammability | Decreases |
| State at room temperature | Gas → Liquid → Solid |

**Why do boiling points increase?**
- Larger molecules have more electrons
- Stronger London dispersion forces (van der Waals forces)
- More energy needed to separate molecules

| Alkane | Number of carbons | Boiling point (°C) |
|--------|-------------------|--------------------|
| Methane | 1 | -162 |
| Ethane | 2 | -89 |
| Propane | 3 | -42 |
| Butane | 4 | 0 |
| Pentane | 5 | 36 |
| Hexane | 6 | 69 |

### Chemical Properties of Alkanes

**Alkanes are relatively unreactive because:**
- Strong C-C and C-H bonds
- Non-polar molecules
- No functional group to attack

**Main reactions:**
1. Combustion (burning)
2. Substitution with halogens (UV light needed)

### Combustion of Alkanes

**Complete combustion:**
- Requires excess oxygen
- Products: carbon dioxide + water
- Releases energy (exothermic)

$$\text{Alkane} + \text{Oxygen} \rightarrow \text{Carbon dioxide} + \text{Water}$$

**Equations:**

$$\text{CH}_4 + 2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_6 + 3\frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Or using whole numbers:
$$2\text{C}_2\text{H}_6 + 7\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 4\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

$$\text{C}_3\text{H}_8 + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 3\text{CO}_2 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Incomplete combustion:**
- Limited oxygen supply
- Products: carbon monoxide + water OR carbon + water
- Produces toxic carbon monoxide (CO)

$$2\text{CH}_4 + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

### Uses of Alkanes

| Alkane | Main uses |
|--------|-----------|
| Methane | Natural gas (heating, cooking) |
| Propane | LPG (camping gas, portable heaters) |
| Butane | LPG, cigarette lighters |
| Octane | Petrol (gasoline) |
| Longer chains | Diesel, lubricating oil, wax |

## Worked Examples

**Example 1:** Write the molecular formula for an alkane with 7 carbon atoms.

**Solution:**
- General formula: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
- n = 7
- Hydrogen atoms = 2(7) + 2 = 16
- Molecular formula: **C₇H₁₆** (heptane)

---

**Example 2:** Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of propane (C₃H₈).

**Solution:**
Step 1: Write the word equation
- Propane + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water

Step 2: Balance carbon atoms
- 3 carbons on left → need 3 CO₂ on right
- C₃H₈ + O₂ → 3CO₂ + H₂O

Step 3: Balance hydrogen atoms
- 8 hydrogens on left → need 4 H₂O on right
- C₃H₈ + O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O

Step 4: Balance oxygen atoms
- Right side: (3 × 2) + 4 = 10 oxygen atoms
- Need 5 O₂ on left

$$\text{C}_3\text{H}_8 + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 3\text{CO}_2 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

---

**Example 3:** Explain why pentane has a higher boiling point than methane.

**Solution:**
- Pentane (C₅H₁₂) is a larger molecule than methane (CH₄)
- Pentane has more electrons than methane
- Larger molecules have stronger London dispersion forces between them
- More energy is needed to overcome these stronger forces
- Therefore, pentane has a higher boiling point
- (Pentane boils at 36°C; methane boils at -162°C)

---

**Example 4:** Draw the displayed formula of butane.

**Solution:**
```
    H   H   H   H
    |   |   |   |
H — C — C — C — C — H
    |   |   |   |
    H   H   H   H
```

- 4 carbon atoms in a chain
- Each carbon makes 4 bonds
- 10 hydrogen atoms total

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Writing C₂H₄ as an alkane
- **Correct:** C₂H₄ is an alkene; ethane is C₂H₆

- **Mistake:** Drawing carbon with wrong number of bonds
- **Correct:** Carbon ALWAYS makes exactly 4 bonds

- **Mistake:** Forgetting to balance combustion equations
- **Correct:** Check: carbons, hydrogens, then oxygens

## Practice Questions

1. Write the molecular formula for an alkane with 6 carbon atoms. (1 mark)

2. Draw the displayed formula of propane. (2 marks)

3. Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of butane (C₄H₁₀). (2 marks)

4. Explain why alkanes are described as saturated hydrocarbons. (2 marks)

5. Describe and explain the trend in boiling points of the alkanes. (4 marks)

6. Explain why incomplete combustion of alkanes is dangerous. (3 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Alkane | A saturated hydrocarbon with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ |
| Saturated | Contains only single carbon-carbon bonds |
| Hydrocarbon | A compound containing only carbon and hydrogen |
| Complete combustion | Burning with excess oxygen to produce CO₂ and H₂O |
| Incomplete combustion | Burning with limited oxygen, producing CO or C |

## Summary

- **Alkanes:** Saturated hydrocarbons, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
- **First four:** Methane, ethane, propane, butane
- **Bonding:** Single C-C and C-H bonds only
- **Physical properties:** Boiling point increases with chain length
- **Relatively unreactive** due to strong C-C and C-H bonds
- **Complete combustion:** Alkane + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O (exothermic)
- **Uses:** Fuels (natural gas, LPG, petrol, diesel)
